lesson.title: Putting It Together: Reading a Graph Near Its Asymptotes
lesson.summary: Combining one-sided limits near a vertical asymptote with limits at infinity gives a complete, precise description of how a function's graph behaves both up close and far away.
lesson.body:
This final section brings together the two families of asymptotic behavior developed so far: local behavior near a vertical asymptote, where x approaches a fixed finite value and the output diverges, and global behavior described by limits at infinity, where x itself runs off toward positive or negative infinity while the output may settle toward a horizontal or oblique asymptote. Combining these two lenses lets you describe every important feature of a graph's shape without plotting a single extra point.

Near a vertical asymptote x = a, the key question is the sign of f(x) on each side of a: does f(x) approach positive infinity or negative infinity as x approaches a from the left, and separately as x approaches a from the right. These two one-sided outcomes can match, both positive infinity or both negative infinity, or they can differ, one positive and one negative, and determining which requires checking the sign of the simplified expression using test points close to a on each side, exactly as was done for vertical asymptotes.

For a full worked example, take f(x) = 1/(x - 3). The denominator vanishes at x = 3 while the numerator, 1, does not, so x = 3 is a vertical asymptote. Testing just to the right, at x = 3.1, gives x - 3 = 0.1, a small positive number, so f(3.1) = 1/0.1 = 10, a large positive value, meaning the limit as x approaches 3 from the right is positive infinity. Testing just to the left, at x = 2.9, gives x - 3 = -0.1, a small negative number, so f(2.9) = 1/(-0.1) = -10, a large negative value, meaning the limit as x approaches 3 from the left is negative infinity. So near x = 3, the graph shoots upward on the right side of the asymptote and plunges downward on the left side.

Now add the global picture. As x approaches infinity, 1/(x - 3) approaches 0, since the denominator grows without bound while the numerator stays fixed at 1, and the same holds as x approaches negative infinity. So y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote in both directions. For large positive x, x - 3 is a large positive number, so 1/(x - 3) is a small positive number, meaning the graph approaches y = 0 from above; for large negative x, x - 3 is a large negative number, so 1/(x - 3) is a small negative number, meaning the graph approaches y = 0 from below.

Putting the local and global pieces together gives the complete shape of the graph without needing graphing software. Coming from the far left, the graph stays just below y = 0, negative and decreasing in value, then plunges toward negative infinity as it approaches x = 3 from the left. On the other side of the asymptote, the graph starts at positive infinity just to the right of x = 3, decreases steadily, and settles down toward y = 0 from above as x moves further to the right. This is exactly the classic two-branch hyperbola shape of 1/x, shifted three units to the right, and every feature of it, the break at x = 3 and the leveling at y = 0, was predicted purely from one-sided and infinite limits, with no trial-and-error plotting required.
